fields.claim_quote: It can also be shown that this proof works for the general [[Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)|ring]] whether it be a [[Definition:Ring with Unity|ring with unity]] or not.
fields.explanation: The final sentence explicitly extends the unchanged proof to rings without unity. The null ring on ℤ/2 is admissible for that extension even though the preceding main statement assumed unity. Over it the full untruncated Cauchy multiplication is identically zero, so no sequence acts as a unit and no square is nonzero; the unit-dependent construction of the displayed proof therefore does not go through as written. This refutes only the literal claim that this same construction/proof works without unity; it does not assert that polynomial rings over non-unital rings cannot be defined or that the isomorphism fails under some other construction, and the theorem proper (ring with unity) is not challenged. No census of small rings is claimed or endorsed.
fields.flaw: The closing claim that the same proof works for a general ring, with or without unity. The displayed proof uses the multiplicative identity 1 of R to form the unity ⟨1,0,0,…⟩ of the sequence ring and the element x = ⟨0,1,0,…⟩ with x² = ⟨0,0,1,0,…⟩; in a ring without unity no multiplicative identity is available to play that role, and for the null ring the key computation fails outright.
fields.witness: R = the null ring on ℤ/2: the additive group {0, 1} with addition mod 2 and a·b = 0 for all a, b (equivalently 2ℤ/4ℤ). It is a ring in the general sense (associativity and distributivity hold trivially since every product is 0) and has no multiplicative identity (1·1 = 0 ≠ 1), so it is a ring without unity, exactly the case the sentence claims the proof covers. Form the proof's own object S = R^(ℕ), the sequences over R with componentwise addition and Cauchy-product multiplication (f·g)_n = Σ_{i+j=n} f_i g_j, over all infinite sequences (no truncation). Three certified conclusions: (1) every Cauchy product is the zero sequence, since each coefficient is a finite sum of products in R, all zero; (2) S has no left multiplicative identity: for the nonzero constant sequence f = ⟨1,1,1,…⟩ every product u·f is the zero sequence ≠ f, so no sequence u acts as an identity; hence no multiplicative identity is available to play the role of the proof's ⟨1,0,0,…⟩ (that tuple is a well-defined sequence, since the additive element 1 of ℤ/2 exists, but it is not a multiplicative identity); (3) no sequence has a nonzero square, so the proof's key computation x² = ⟨0,0,1,0,…⟩ ≠ 0 for x = ⟨0,1,0,…⟩ fails. The selected Lean theorem certifies exactly these three statements for the NonUnitalCommRing on ZMod 2 with zero multiplication and the full-sequence Cauchy product: (∀ f g, cauchy f g = 0) ∧ ¬(∃ u, ∀ f, cauchy u f = f) ∧ ¬(∃ f, cauchy f f ≠ 0).
